s: Part two.
Escalation and ambiguity.

By the end of this part, you'll know which triggers should send a case to a human, why a request for a human is its own rule, how many clarifying questions an agent gets, and what to do when the policy itself has a hole.
Let's start with a picture.
Every organisation that lets people act on their own also tells them when to fetch someone senior.
The versions that work describe the situation.
Not the person's feelings.
Imagine a shop manager who tells staff, "call me whenever a customer sounds angry."
She spends the whole day on easy returns.
Meanwhile, a genuinely unusual case slips through, because a clerk improvised.
Now try a different rule.
"Call me when the customer asks for me, when our policy does not cover it, or when you have tried everything."
That one gets her to the right cases.
And "come and get me if you are unsure" is worse still.
Why?
Because it turns the trigger into a fact about the clerk's mood that day.
Not a fact about the case.
The technical name for this is escalation criteria.
And the exam wants them checkable against the record.
The valid triggers come in four kinds.
One.
An explicit request for a human.
Two.
A policy gap.
That means no rule matches, or two playbooks conflict.
Three.
Being genuinely stuck after reasonable attempts.
Tools exhausted, and no progress.
Four.
A hard tier, for safety or legal risk, and for irreversible or high-consequence actions.
The rules are evaluated in order.
The first match wins.
And the system records which rule fired, on the ticket.
That record is what makes the policy auditable and revisable.
Without it, nobody can explain afterwards why any ticket was, or was not, escalated.
The study notes lay out a sample rule set, in tiers.
Let's walk down it.
First, a hard-escalate tier.
Here, no automated reply is sent at all.
It covers safety or self-harm.
A legal threat.
An explicit request for a human, a manager or a callback.
An active regulatory complaint, chargeback or subpoena.
An action that would move funds, close an account, or change contract terms.
And enterprise-tier or high-value accounts.
Second, an escalate-after-one-attempt tier.
Third, proceed automatically.
But only when the intent matches a documented playbook, every required field is present, and no escalation condition matched.
Fourth, ask one clarifying question.
And finally, an abstention path.
We'll get to that one.
One tension to flag.
That sample rule set lists money-moving actions in the hard tier.
Yet the practice questions have the agent resolve policy-covered refunds on its own.
So read the sample as a threshold choice.
Like the notes' own example: "any refund over five hundred dollars."
On the exam, follow the stem.
If the scenario says the playbook covers the case, resolving it automatically is correct.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A support agent escalates any ticket with a strongly negative sentiment score.
The human queue is overloaded with angry customers whose refunds were fully covered by policy.
Meanwhile, a partial refund on a bundled item, which no playbook covered, was handled automatically, with a guessed amount.
The lead wants two things.
Fewer escalations.
And fewer unsafe automated actions.
What's the best answer?
Take a second.
The answer.
Escalate only on checkable triggers: an explicit human request, a policy gap, or no progress.
And resolve covered cases even when the customer is upset.
That single change does both jobs.
It cuts the angry-but-covered volume.
And it catches the bundle case.
Now the wrong turns.
Each one is a different unreliable proxy.
Wrong: raise the sentiment threshold, and add a policy-gap check as a secondary signal.
Why?
It's still escalating on mood.
And the right signal has been demoted.
Wrong: add a self-assessed confidence score, and escalate below seven out of ten.
Why?
Self-reported confidence is noise.
Formalising it into a number keeps the volatility.
Wrong: escalate anything needing more than three lookups or two policy conditions.
Why?
Complexity alone is not a trigger.
Complex cases call for care, not handoff.
A second practice scenario from the notes adds two more symptoms worth memorising.
Symptom one.
Escalation volume swinging between eight and thirty-four percent over three weeks, with no change in the ticket mix.
Symptom two.
A support lead who cannot tell an auditor why any ticket was escalated.
What do they point to?
Swinging volume points to a self-report trigger.
Unexplainable decisions point to no recorded rule.
The fix is the same as before.
Ordered, checkable conditions.
An explicit rule for human requests.
And an abstention path.
That scenario has two more wrong turns.
Wrong: a fixed escalation quota, say fifteen percent a week.
Why?
It makes escalation depend on how many tickets arrived earlier in the week.
And it can suppress a genuine hard case.
Wrong: review everything for thirty days, in order to refine the wording of the confidence instruction.
Why?
That keeps the trigger inside the model's self-assessment.
Now a source disagreement you should know about.
The lesson eighteen deck says customer sentiment is never an escalation trigger.
The study notes' sample rule set allows it, in the second tier.
Escalate after one resolution attempt, if sentiment is negative on two consecutive customer turns.
Here's the good news.
Both sources agree on the part the exam tests.
Sentiment alone is the wrong trigger.
Explicit criteria, plus an explicit request for a human, are the right ones.
So.
If a question offers sentiment as the sole or primary trigger, it's wrong.
If a question frames sentiment as a secondary signal, after a failed resolution attempt, answer in the question's terms.
Hold on to this line.
Escalate on facts you can check against the record.
Never on mood, complexity, or self-reported confidence.
The request for a human deserves its own segment.
The exam treats it as a separate axis.
The plain version.
If a customer asks to speak to a person, they get a person.
Even if the machine would have handled it perfectly, and faster.
It's not a question of how risky the request is.
It's a question of what the customer agreed to.
In exam terms, an explicit request for a human is a hard escalation.
It's evaluated before any playbook match.
And there's a list of things you don't do.
No automated reply sent first.
No attempt to resolve it.
No asking why.
And no pushing the customer to a self-service portal.
The notes call stated preference a separate axis from severity.
Severity measures the consequence of getting the request wrong.
Preference measures consent.
A system that overrides a stated preference, because it calculated the request as low risk, has substituted its own judgment for the customer's.
The trap is a stem that tells you the automation succeeds ninety-nine percent of the time, and the customer would probably be satisfied.
That number is irrelevant.
Which is the whole point.
The failure from overriding is not a wrong answer.
It's a trust breach.
Sometimes a compliance breach.
And it surfaces in a complaint, rather than a metric.
Takeaway.
A customer who asks for a human gets a human, immediately.
Next, ambiguity.
What should the agent do when the request itself is unclear?
The plain version.
A waiter hears "I'll have the special" on a night with two specials.
He asks once.
The fish, or the risotto?
He doesn't guess.
And he doesn't fire off ten questions.
If the answer is still unclear, he fetches the manager, rather than turning dinner into an interview.
The technical name is a bounded clarification budget.
Three conditions switch it on.
The intent matches a playbook.
Exactly one required field is missing or ambiguous.
And the customer can supply it directly.
Then the agent asks one specific clarifying question, and re-evaluates the rules.
The limit is one clarifying question per ticket.
A second ambiguity routes to a human.
The notes put the reasoning memorably.
Hold on to this line.
Clarifying questions are cheap individually, and corrosive in aggregate.
Why?
Because a system that asks three questions before doing anything has moved the work back onto the customer.
While still charging them the wait.
Question two.
This one is select two.
Here's the scenario.
A customer writes, "please refund my order, it arrived broken."
The account has two orders delivered this week.
The playbook needs an order ID.
Everything else is present.
Which two behaviours are correct?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, ask one question, naming both candidate orders.
Second, if the reply is still ambiguous, route to a human, rather than asking again.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: refund the most recent order.
Why?
That's a guess on a money-moving action.
It produces a confident wrong refund, and the customer finds it, not you.
Wrong: escalate immediately, because any ambiguity means uncertainty.
Why?
That's over-escalation.
Wrong: collect the order ID, damage photos, refund method and a reason code, all in one message.
Why?
That's interrogation.
It asks for fields the playbook does not need.
Takeaway.
One missing field the customer can supply earns one question.
A second ambiguity earns a human.
Now the contrast the exam builds its hardest escalation questions on.
Ambiguity in the request, versus ambiguity in the policy.
The plain version.
A new cashier finds two store rules that contradict each other, for one return.
Quietly picking one hides the problem.
Asking the customer which rule they prefer also hides it.
Because the customer cannot settle a contradiction in the rulebook.
The right move?
Call the supervisor.
And add the case to a list the manager reads every week, so the rulebook gets fixed.
The technical name is the abstention path.
The notes describe it as the escape hatch, not a failure state.
When does it apply?
Three situations.
When no rule matched.
When two playbooks match with conflicting actions.
Or when the required action is not covered by any playbook.
Then the agent routes the case to the human queue, with a reason code of policy_gap.
It attaches three things.
The ticket.
The playbooks it considered.
And the specific decision it could not make.
That makes the case fast for a human to decide.
And there are things it doesn't do.
It doesn't guess.
And it doesn't send a holding reply that implies a resolution.
Finally, the volume in that queue is reviewed weekly, as the input to the next policy revision.
Why weekly review?
Because a queue nobody reviews collects the evidence of a policy gap, and changes nothing.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A damaged clearance item matches two playbooks.
The warranty playbook says replace.
The clearance playbook says final sale, store credit only.
Leadership wants each case handled safely.
And it also wants to learn how often the policy is incomplete.
What should the agent do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Abstain, with a policy-gap reason, both playbooks attached, and weekly review.
That second goal, learning how often the policy is incomplete, is what points at the weekly review.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: apply the cheaper playbook.
Why?
It's still a guess.
And it hides the gap.
Wrong: ask the customer to choose.
Why?
That's a clarifying question masking a policy problem.
Wrong: escalate, while telling the customer the replacement has been approved.
Why?
That's exactly the prohibited holding reply.
So when do you ask, when do you escalate, and when do you proceed?
Three options, each with a cost and a risk.
Proceed when a playbook matches and everything is present.
The cost is one model turn.
The risk of choosing wrongly is a confident wrong action, found by the customer.
Ask one question when exactly one input is missing, and the customer can supply it.
The cost is a round trip.
The risk is interrogation loops, or masking a policy problem.
Escalate for hard-tier conditions, an explicit request, or no matching policy.
The cost is human time and queue latency.
And the risk of overdoing it is a drowned queue, where reviewers start rubber-stamping, and the control you paid for quietly disappears.
That last point, over-escalation as its own failure, is tested directly.
That's part two.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
A gap in the policy is never the customer's question to answer.
Abstain, file it, and review it weekly.
And this connects forward.
In a multi-agent system, the thing that most often needs escalating is not a customer.
It's a subagent that could not do its job.
Coming up in part three: error propagation across multi-agent systems.
